common_name: Wolf Plum (Historic Iowa Native American Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or grafted stock while still dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Wolf is not self-fruitful and needs a second American plum nearby.

directions: Site in full sun on well-drained soil and pair with a second American plum seedling or named cultivar, since Wolf will not set a useful crop on its own. Wolf was selected from wild stock in Iowa during the late 19th-century prairie plum boom and was carried on USDA horticulturist W.A. Kerr's influential list of over a hundred promising native plum selections gathered from Midwest farms and nurseries. Its round, thick-skinned red fruit ripens in mid- to late summer and holds up well for cooking into jams, butters, and preserves. Like most native plum selections of its era, it suckers from the root to form a spreading thicket unless suckers are removed, and it tolerates the cold, drought, and heavy clay soils of the northern plains far better than introduced plum species.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical plum variety records
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
University of Minnesota Fruit Research

common_name: Hawkeye Plum (H.A. Terry Iowa Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted stock in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained soil, siting a second American plum cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Grow in full sun on well-drained soil with a compatible American plum planted nearby, since Hawkeye is self-incompatible and will not fruit reliably alone. Hawkeye was introduced around 1882 by pioneering Iowa plum breeder H.A. Terry of Crescent, Iowa, one of the most prolific selectors of native plum during the 19th-century Midwest plum-breeding era, and it became one of the more widely distributed named American plum varieties of its time. The medium to large fruit ripens red over yellow flesh with a sweet-tart flavor well suited to fresh eating as well as canning and preserves. As with other heirloom American plum selections, expect root suckering that can be managed by removing unwanted sprouts, and expect the tree to tolerate harsh winters and drought far better than European or Japanese plum types.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical plum variety records
American Pomological Society historical fruit catalog records

common_name: Terry Plum (H.A. Terry Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted stock in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Terry requires a different American plum cultivar nearby to set fruit.

directions: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil alongside a second American plum for cross-pollination, since this variety sets little to no fruit without a compatible pollen source nearby. Terry originated from the plum-breeding work of H.A. Terry of Crescent, Iowa, one of the era's most active selectors of native American plum, and was distributed alongside his other introductions during the 19th-century prairie plum boom; it was later used as a parent in early Prunus salicina x americana hybridizing programs in the northern plains. The fruit is medium-sized with the tangy, rich flavor typical of well-selected native plum, good for fresh eating once fully ripe and excellent cooked into jams and sauces. Like other heirloom native plum selections, it suckers from the roots and shrugs off cold, drought, and poor soil that would damage most orchard fruit trees.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical plum variety records
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
South Dakota State University historical fruit breeding records

common_name: Princess Kay Flowering Plum (Double-Flowered Canada Plum)

planting.note: Plant grafted or containerized stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this cultivar is grown purely as an ornamental flowering tree and does not need a pollinator since it sets no fruit.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil where its extreme cold hardiness can be put to use in far northern landscapes that cannot support most other flowering plums. Princess Kay was discovered as a wild sport with fully double flowers in Itasca County, Minnesota, by Catherine Kay and Robert Nyland, and was released by the University of Minnesota in 1986 as an ornamental selection of the native Canada plum. Unlike the species and unlike fruiting native plum cultivars, it produces no fruit and needs no cross-pollinator, since its double, fragrant white flowers that age to pale pink are sterile; the tradeoff is an exceptionally showy, weeks-long spring bloom set off by smooth blackish bark. Because it is a Canada plum selection, it tolerates winter cold to roughly -40 degrees Fahrenheit that would kill most other ornamental flowering trees.
sources: University of Minnesota Landscape Arboretum
Minnesota Nursery and Landscape Association
University of Minnesota Extension

common_name: Premier Beach Plum (Plum Island Named Beach Plum Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted stock in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a second beach plum cultivar such as Eastham or Hancock for cross-pollination.

directions: Site in sandy, salt-spray-exposed, well-drained soil in full sun and plant beside a different named beach plum cultivar, since seedling beach plum stands and single clones fruit poorly without a cross-pollinator. Premier was selected on Plum Island, Massachusetts, during the early-to-mid 20th-century burst of interest in developing beach plum as a commercial New England crop, and it was long regarded as one of the best-flavored named selections available, though it is more prone to brown rot than some of its contemporaries. Its fruit ripens in late summer to a deep purple color prized for jams, jellies, and the traditional Cape Cod and Long Island beach plum preserves. As a true coastal native shrub, it withstands salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soil that would stress or kill most other fruiting plants, and light pruning after flowering is enough to keep it productive.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension beach plum research
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program
Rutgers Cooperative Extension

common_name: Hancock Beach Plum (Fort Hancock Named Beach Plum Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted stock in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun near a different beach plum cultivar such as Eastham or Squibnocket for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained, salt-spray-exposed soil in full sun with a second named beach plum cultivar nearby, since this species sets fruit poorly without cross-pollination. Hancock was selected near Fort Hancock, New Jersey, during the early-to-mid 20th-century push to develop beach plum into a viable commercial fruit crop for coastal growers, and it is valued for its early ripening and blue-skinned fruit. The fruit is well suited to jellies, jams, and syrups, ripening earlier than many other named beach plum selections, which can help extend a home harvest season when grown alongside later cultivars. Being a true dune shrub, it thrives in poor sandy soil and salt-laden wind that would damage most other fruiting plants, and it needs only light post-bloom pruning to stay productive and shapely.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension beach plum research
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program
University of Maryland Extension

common_name: Bassett Beach Plum (Bassett's American, Earliest Named Beach Plum)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a second beach plum cultivar for cross-pollination, since this heirloom selection is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Grow in sandy, well-drained, salt-exposed soil in full sun and site a second beach plum cultivar nearby to ensure fruit set. Known historically as Bassett's American, this New Jersey selection was recognized as one of only a couple of named beach plum cultivars documented by pomologist U.P. Hedrick in his 1911 survey of American plums, making it among the earliest fruit-improved selections of the species on record. It was chosen for producing noticeably larger fruit than typical wild seedling beach plum stands, harvested in late summer for jams, jellies, and preserves. As a true coastal dune native, it tolerates salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soils that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, and it needs only light pruning after bloom to remain productive.
sources: Hedrick, U.P., The Plums of New York (1911), New York Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program
Cornell University Cooperative Extension beach plum research
